Fig 1 (p4–5). Title: ‘Without Reforms to the City’s Zoning Code, Permitting Requests from Now Until 2041 Will Likely Be Concentrated In and Around Chicago’s Near Northwest Neighborhoods’. Subtitle: ‘Estimated probability of a permit for new housing development being requested on a given parcel by 2041, based on the Urban Institute’s Housing Market Forecaster’. Sources: ‘Authors’ analysis of Cook County Assessor parcel data, City of Chicago zoning data, and 2020–24 census tract–level American Community Survey data.’ Notes: ‘These estimates assume the city makes no changes to its zoning code and permits continue at the same pace as they did from 2011 to 2025 under the same economic conditions. Estimates are for cumulative development from 2026 to 2041.’ (labels ‘Sources:’ / ‘Notes:’ in bold)

Fig 2 (p6–7). Title: ‘Under Chicago’s Current Zoning, Most Housing Units Permitted Between Now and 2041 Will Likely Be Concentrated In and Around the City’s Downtown’. Subtitle: ‘Estimated housing unit permits per ward by 2041, based on the Urban Institute’s Housing Market Forecaster’. Sources and Notes: word for word the same as Fig 1.

Fig 3 (p10–13). Title: ‘Combining Reforms That Allow Small-Scale Apartments Plus Transit-Oriented Upzoning Would Unlock More Housing Supply Across the City’. Subtitle: ‘Estimated additional units permitted by 2041, compared with baseline, by reform’. Panel labels: ‘Reform 1: Allowing duplexes and triplexes’ (p10, above map p10); ‘Reform 2: Legalizing small apartment buildings (four to nine units)’ (bottom of p10, map p11); ‘Reform 3: Enabling higher-density multifamily buildings within ¼ mile of transit’ (bottom of p11, map p12); ‘Reform 4: Combining reforms 2 and 3’ (bottom of p12, map p13). Sources (p13): same text as Fig 1. Notes (p13): ‘These estimates assume economic conditions between 2011 and 2025 persist. Estimates are for cumulative development from 2026 to 2041.’
